stories.title: The first cities of Sumer
stories.blurb: How did farming villages in southern Iraq become the first cities, with writing, kings and empires?

steps.name: Uruk period
steps.what: Uruk grows into a city of perhaps tens of thousands of people around the Eanna and Anu temple precincts.
steps.why: It is usually taken as the first true city, the model for everything that follows.

steps.name: Proto-cuneiform
steps.what: Temple scribes at Uruk press signs into clay tablets to record rations, livestock and workers.
steps.why: Writing begins as bookkeeping for a large urban economy, not as literature.

steps.name: Jemdet Nasr period
steps.what: Administrative tablets at Jemdet Nasr list goods from several cities, sealed with shared city seals.
steps.why: It shows the cities of the plain already tied together by trade and common institutions.

steps.name: Royal Cemetery at Ur
steps.what: Queen Puabi is buried at Ur with gold, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan and dozens of attendants.
steps.why: The wealth and far-traveled goods show how much surplus and long-distance trade the city-states commanded.

steps.name: Stele of the Vultures
steps.what: Eannatum of Lagash records his victory over neighbouring Umma in a long dispute over border fields and canals.
steps.why: City-states fought over water and farmland; this is among the earliest recorded wars.

steps.name: Ebla tablets
steps.what: The palace archive of Ebla in Syria, about 17,000 tablet pieces, records textiles, metals and diplomacy in cuneiform.
steps.why: Sumerian writing and bureaucracy had spread far up the Euphrates trade routes.

steps.name: Reforms of Urukagina
steps.what: Urukagina of Lagash claims to cut taxes and fees and protect widows and orphans from the powerful.
steps.why: It is the first known attempt by a ruler to justify power through social reform.

steps.name: Sargon conquers Sumer
steps.what: Sargon of Akkad defeats Lugal-zage-si of Uruk and brings the Sumerian cities under one king.
steps.why: The Akkadian Empire is the first state to rule many cities from one capital.

steps.name: Enheduanna at Ur
steps.what: Sargon's daughter Enheduanna serves as high priestess of the moon god at Ur and composes temple hymns.
steps.why: She is the first author known by name, and her post tied the conquered south to the dynasty.

steps.name: Naram-Sin and Nippur
steps.what: Naram-Sin, Sargon's grandson, calls himself god and king of the four quarters; later tradition blamed him for desecrating Nippur's temple.
steps.why: Empire brought new claims of divine kingship, and later Sumerians remembered it as overreach.

steps.name: Gutian rule
steps.what: After Akkad weakens, Gutians from the Zagros mountains take power over parts of Sumer for several decades.
steps.why: The first empire collapsed fast, leaving the cities to local rulers and outsiders.

steps.name: Gudea of Lagash
steps.what: Gudea rebuilds the Eninnu temple at Girsu with cedar from Lebanon and stone from Magan, and has dozens of diorite statues carved.
steps.why: Local city-states kept prospering and trading even without an empire.

steps.name: Ziggurat of Ur
steps.what: Ur-Nammu founds the Third Dynasty of Ur and builds a great stepped temple tower for the moon god Nanna.
steps.why: Ur III rebuilt a unified state in the south with monumental religion at its centre.

steps.name: Code of Ur-Nammu
steps.what: The oldest surviving law code sets fixed fines in silver for injuries.
steps.why: Written law shows how far administration had come since the first tablets.

steps.name: Puzrish-Dagan
steps.what: King Shulgi founds a livestock centre near Nippur that logs tens of thousands of animals received as taxes and offerings.
steps.why: Ur III was one of history's most bureaucratic states, with every sheep on a tablet.

steps.name: Fall of Ur
steps.what: Elamites sack Ur and carry its last king Ibbi-Sin off to Elam, ending the Third Dynasty.
steps.why: The end of Sumerian rule; later scribes mourned it in the Lament for Ur.

stories.title: The pyramid age
stories.blurb: How did Old Kingdom Egypt build the pyramids, and why did its central state fall apart?

steps.name: Pyramid of Djoser
steps.what: Djoser's official Imhotep stacks six stone mastabas into the first large stone building, the Step Pyramid.
steps.why: It marks the start of monumental stone building and of the state that could organise it.

steps.name: Bent Pyramid
steps.what: Sneferu's builders change the slope halfway up when the structure shows strain, then build the true Red Pyramid nearby.
steps.why: Pyramid building was learned by trial and error over a single long reign.

steps.name: Great Pyramid of Giza
steps.what: Khufu's pyramid rises about 146 metres from roughly 2.3 million blocks.
steps.why: The peak of the state's power to mobilise labour, food and stone.

steps.name: Diary of Merer
steps.what: An inspector named Merer logs his crew's trips carrying limestone from Tura down the Nile to Giza; the papyri were found at a Red Sea harbour.
steps.why: The oldest inscribed papyri show the logistics behind the pyramid: boats, canals and rations.

steps.name: Great Sphinx of Giza
steps.what: The Sphinx is carved from the bedrock beside Khafre's pyramid causeway.
steps.why: Royal building turned the whole Giza plateau into a cult landscape for dead kings.

steps.name: Abusir Papyri
steps.what: Temple accounts at Abusir record duty rosters, offerings and equipment for the cults of Fifth Dynasty kings.
steps.why: They show the everyday running of royal temples, which absorbed land and labour across Egypt.

steps.name: Pyramid Texts
steps.what: Spells for the king's afterlife are carved inside the small pyramid of Unas, the first such texts.
steps.why: Pyramids got smaller as religious texts and temples took more of the resources.

steps.name: Reign of Pepi II
steps.what: Pepi II is said to reign for over 60 years, perhaps up to 94, while provincial nomarchs gain power.
steps.why: A very long reign with a weakening court left a succession crisis at its end.

steps.name: Autobiography of Harkhuf
steps.what: Harkhuf, governor at Aswan, leads donkey caravans south to the land of Yam and records a letter from the boy king Pepi II.
steps.why: Provincial governors grew rich and independent through trade and long careers far from the capital.

steps.name: 4.2-kiloyear event
steps.what: A long dry period weakens the Nile floods across the region.
steps.why: Low floods meant failed harvests, which undermined royal legitimacy and stores.

steps.name: First Intermediate Period
steps.what: Rulers at Herakleopolis claim kingship in the north while Thebes rises in the south.
steps.why: The unified Old Kingdom state had broken into competing centres.

steps.name: Ankhtifi's famine inscriptions
steps.what: The nomarch Ankhtifi claims in his tomb that all Upper Egypt starved while he fed his own province.
steps.why: Local strongmen now took credit for feeding people, the job once claimed by the king.

steps.name: Reunification by Mentuhotep II
steps.what: Mentuhotep II of Thebes defeats Herakleopolis and reunites Egypt, founding the Middle Kingdom.
steps.why: The collapse ended in a new unified state, governed from the south.

stories.title: The Indus cities
stories.blurb: Who built the planned cities of the Indus valley, how did they trade with Mesopotamia, and why did they fade?

steps.name: Early Harappan Kot Diji
steps.what: Fortified farming towns like Kot Diji appear along the Indus with wheel-made pottery.
steps.why: The urban phase grew out of centuries of village life in the river plains.

steps.name: Harappa
steps.what: Harappa on the Ravi grows into a city of brick houses, drains and standard-size bricks.
steps.why: The mature Harappan phase begins, with uniform planning over a huge area.

steps.name: Rakhigarhi
steps.what: Rakhigarhi in the Ghaggar plain becomes one of the largest Indus settlements.
steps.why: The civilisation spread east well beyond the Indus itself.

steps.name: Great Bath
steps.what: Builders at Mohenjo-daro line a 12 by 7 metre pool with fitted brick and bitumen.
steps.why: A large public structure with no clear palace suggests an unusual, less monarchic city.

steps.name: Indus script
steps.what: Short inscriptions appear on stamp seals used to mark goods.
steps.why: The script is still undeciphered, so the people can be read only through objects.

steps.name: Dholavira
steps.what: On an island in the Rann of Kutch, Dholavira cuts large reservoirs to store seasonal water.
steps.why: Water engineering let cities survive in dry margins.

steps.name: Lothal dockyard
steps.what: Lothal in Gujarat has a large brick basin, often read as a dock, and bead workshops.
steps.why: Coastal towns linked the Indus to sea trade across the Arabian Sea.

steps.name: Meluhha in Akkadian texts
steps.what: Sargon of Akkad boasts that ships from Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun moored at his capital.
steps.why: Mesopotamian texts name the Indus region as Meluhha, a source of carnelian, wood and ivory.

steps.name: Magan copper
steps.what: Indus pottery and seals reach coastal Oman, the copper-producing land of Magan.
steps.why: The Gulf was a shared trade zone, with Oman as a stop between India and Iraq.

steps.name: Dilmun
steps.what: Dilmun on Bahrain acts as a middleman port, using weights on the Indus standard.
steps.why: Gulf merchants carried Indus goods into Mesopotamia in the Ur III period and after.

steps.name: Shortugai
steps.what: An Indus trading outpost on the Amu Darya in northern Afghanistan, near the lapis lazuli mines of Badakhshan.
steps.why: Indus traders reached far into Central Asia for raw materials.

steps.name: Drying of the Ghaggar-Hakra
steps.what: Weaker monsoons and shifting rivers reduce water in the Ghaggar-Hakra system.
steps.why: Changing rivers and climate are the leading explanation for urban decline.

steps.name: Decline of Mohenjo-daro
steps.what: Mohenjo-daro shrinks, building quality falls and the city is largely abandoned.
steps.why: The big cities emptied while people moved east into smaller villages.

steps.name: Cemetery H culture
steps.what: A new style of pottery and burial appears at Harappa in the Late Harappan phase.
steps.why: Life continued in the region, but without the cities, seals or long-distance trade.

steps.name: End of the Late Harappan phase
steps.what: By about 1300 BCE the last traces of the Harappan tradition fade into regional village cultures.
steps.why: The civilisation did not end in one catastrophe; it dissolved over centuries.

stories.title: The Late Bronze Age collapse
stories.blurb: Why did the connected palace kingdoms of the eastern Mediterranean collapse around 1200 BCE?

steps.name: Amarna letters
steps.what: Clay letters in Akkadian pass between Egypt and the kings of Babylon, Mitanni, Hatti, Assyria and Cyprus, who call each other brother.
steps.why: They show a club of great powers bound by gifts, marriages and trade.

steps.name: Uluburun shipwreck
steps.what: A ship sinks off southern Turkey with about ten tons of Cypriot copper, a ton of tin, glass ingots and goods from a dozen cultures.
steps.why: The system ran on long-distance metal trade, which made it fragile.

steps.name: Battle of Kadesh
steps.what: Ramesses II and the Hittite king Muwatalli II fight a huge chariot battle in Syria that neither clearly wins.
steps.why: The great powers were evenly matched and spent heavily on war.

steps.name: Egyptian-Hittite peace treaty
steps.what: Egypt and Hatti sign the earliest surviving peace treaty, copied in hieroglyphs and in Akkadian.
steps.why: Peace between the giants kept trade flowing for two more generations.

steps.name: Lion Gate
steps.what: Mycenae enlarges its walls and builds the Lion Gate.
steps.why: Heavier fortifications hint at rising insecurity in the Greek palace world.

steps.name: Merneptah Stele
steps.what: Merneptah records defeating Libyans and allied northern peoples who invaded the western Delta.
steps.why: The first wave of migrating groups was already pressing on Egypt.

steps.name: Destruction of Emar
steps.what: Emar, a Hittite-ruled trade town on the Euphrates, is destroyed; its dated tablets help fix the collapse.
steps.why: Inland towns fell too, not only coastal ones.

steps.name: Fall of Ugarit
steps.what: Ugarit is destroyed; its last king Ammurapi had written that enemy ships were burning his towns while his own fleet was away.
steps.why: The richest trading port of the Levant disappeared and never recovered.

steps.name: Destruction of the Palace of Nestor
steps.what: The palace at Pylos burns; the fire bakes its Linear B tablets, which record rowers and coast watchers.
steps.why: Greek palace states collapsed along with their writing system.

steps.name: Abandonment of Hattusa
steps.what: The Hittite capital is emptied and later burned, after years of grain shortages and civil strife.
steps.why: An empire that had matched Egypt vanished within a generation.

steps.name: Battle of the Delta
steps.what: Ramesses III defeats the Sea Peoples in a land and river battle at the mouths of the Nile.
steps.why: Egypt survived the collapse, but at heavy cost.

steps.name: Medinet Habu reliefs
steps.what: Ramesses III's mortuary temple shows the Sea Peoples with families and ox carts as well as warships.
steps.why: The reliefs are key evidence that whole populations were on the move.

steps.name: Deir el-Medina strike
steps.what: Royal tomb builders at Deir el-Medina stop work when their grain rations are months late.
steps.why: The first recorded strike shows the strain on Egypt's economy after the collapse.

stories.title: Assyria, Babylon and Persia
stories.blurb: How did one empire after another rule the Near East, from Assyria's rise to Cyrus taking Babylon?

steps.name: Accession of Tiglath-Pileser III
steps.what: Tiglath-Pileser III seizes the throne at Kalhu and builds a standing army and a system of provinces.
steps.why: His reforms turned Assyria from a raiding power into a governing empire.

steps.name: Fall of Samaria
steps.what: Assyria takes Samaria after a three-year siege and deports thousands of Israelites.
steps.why: Mass deportation was Assyria's tool to break resistance and resettle labour.

steps.name: Dur-Sharrukin
steps.what: Sargon II starts building a new capital from scratch, with palaces lined with carved reliefs.
steps.why: The empire's wealth paid for whole new cities; this one was abandoned after his death.

steps.name: Siege of Lachish
steps.what: Sennacherib storms the Judean city of Lachish and later shows the siege on his palace walls at Nineveh.
steps.why: Assyria punished revolt with exemplary violence and made it propaganda.

steps.name: Destruction of Babylon
steps.what: After years of Babylonian revolts, Sennacherib sacks Babylon and floods parts of it.
steps.why: Babylon was the empire's hardest problem, and its resentment outlived Assyria.

steps.name: Assyrian conquest of Egypt
steps.what: Esarhaddon takes Memphis and drives out the Kushite pharaoh Taharqa.
steps.why: Assyria reached its greatest extent, stretching from Iran to the Nile.

steps.name: Library of Ashurbanipal
steps.what: Ashurbanipal collects tens of thousands of tablets at Nineveh, including the Epic of Gilgamesh.
steps.why: Much of what is known of Mesopotamian literature survives because this library burned and baked its tablets.

steps.name: Nabopolassar takes Babylon
steps.what: Nabopolassar, a Chaldean leader, is crowned king in Babylon and throws off Assyrian rule.
steps.why: The revolt began the end of Assyria after a civil war over its throne.

steps.name: Fall of Nineveh
steps.what: Babylonians and Medes take and sack Nineveh after a siege of about three months.
steps.why: The capital of the largest empire yet fell in one summer.

steps.name: Battle of Carchemish
steps.what: Crown prince Nebuchadnezzar defeats Egypt and the last Assyrian remnants on the Euphrates.
steps.why: Babylon inherited Assyria's western lands.

steps.name: Siege of Jerusalem
steps.what: Nebuchadnezzar destroys Jerusalem and its temple and deports much of Judah's elite to Babylon.
steps.why: Babylon used Assyrian methods; the exile reshaped Jewish religion.

steps.name: Ishtar Gate
steps.what: Nebuchadnezzar rebuilds Babylon with blue glazed brick gates, walls and the Esagila temple.
steps.why: Tribute from the empire made Babylon the largest city of its day.

steps.name: Nabonidus at Tayma
steps.what: King Nabonidus leaves Babylon and lives about ten years at the Arabian oasis of Tayma, on the incense routes.
steps.why: His absence and religious choices alienated Babylon's priests just as Persia rose.

steps.name: Cyrus defeats Astyages
steps.what: Cyrus of Persia defeats his Median overlord Astyages and takes the Median kingdom.
steps.why: A small Persian kingdom became the heir to the Median empire.

steps.name: Siege of Sardis
steps.what: Cyrus captures Sardis and the Lydian king Croesus, whose kingdom had pioneered coinage.
steps.why: Persia gained Anatolia and the Greek cities of the coast.

steps.name: Fall of Babylon
steps.what: After winning at Opis, Persian forces enter Babylon without a long siege; Cyrus presents himself as restorer of its gods.
steps.why: Persia absorbed the last Mesopotamian empire and ruled it through local traditions.

stories.title: Greeks and Persians
stories.blurb: How did Athens beat Persia, build an empire on silver and ships, and then lose it to Sparta?

steps.name: Ionian Revolt
steps.what: Aristagoras of Miletus leads the Greek cities of Ionia in revolt against Persia, with help from Athens and Eretria.
steps.why: Athenian help drew Persian revenge onto mainland Greece.

steps.name: Battle of Lade
steps.what: The Persian fleet crushes the Ionian fleet off Miletus, and Miletus is sacked.
steps.why: The revolt ended, and Darius turned to punishing Athens.

steps.name: Battle of Marathon
steps.what: About 10,000 Athenians and Plataeans defeat a Persian landing force.
steps.why: A democracy's citizen army proved it could beat Persia.

steps.name: Laurion silver strike
steps.what: A rich new silver vein is found at Laurion; Themistocles persuades Athens to spend it on about 200 triremes.
steps.why: Slave-mined silver paid for the navy that saved Athens and then built its empire.

steps.name: Battle of Thermopylae
steps.what: Leonidas and a few thousand Greeks hold the pass for three days before being outflanked.
steps.why: The delay let the Greek fleet regroup while Xerxes marched on Athens.

steps.name: Battle of Salamis
steps.what: The Greek fleet, mostly Athenian, defeats the larger Persian fleet in the straits.
steps.why: The silver-built navy won the war at sea.

steps.name: Battle of Plataea
steps.what: A Greek army led by Sparta defeats the Persian land army and kills Mardonius.
steps.why: Persia never invaded mainland Greece again.

steps.name: Delian League
steps.what: Aegean cities form an alliance under Athens, paying ships or silver into a treasury on Delos.
steps.why: The alliance slowly became an Athenian empire funded by tribute.

steps.name: Long Walls
steps.what: Athens joins the city to its port Piraeus with walls about six kilometres long.
steps.why: With grain coming by sea, Athens could survive a land siege as long as it ruled the waves.

steps.name: Parthenon
steps.what: Work begins on the Parthenon, partly funded by League tribute moved to Athens in 454.
steps.why: Imperial revenue paid for the monuments of classical Athens.

steps.name: Plague of Athens
steps.what: An epidemic enters through Piraeus into a city crowded with refugees from the countryside, killing perhaps a quarter of the people.
steps.why: Pericles' strategy of hiding behind the walls made the plague worse; he died of it in 429.

steps.name: Battle of Pylos
steps.what: Athenians trap and capture about 120 Spartan citizens on Sphacteria.
steps.why: Sparta's shortage of citizens made the captives a powerful bargaining chip.

steps.name: Sicilian Expedition
steps.what: Athens sends a huge fleet to attack Syracuse; by 413 the whole force is destroyed.
steps.why: The disaster cost Athens most of its fleet and manpower.

steps.name: Spartan fort at Decelea
steps.what: Sparta fortifies Decelea in Attica year-round; Thucydides says over 20,000 slaves ran away, many from the silver mines.
steps.why: Cutting off Laurion silver and farm income starved Athens of money.

steps.name: Battle of Aegospotami
steps.what: Lysander, with Persian money, captures almost the whole Athenian fleet at the Hellespont.
steps.why: Without its fleet Athens could no longer import grain.

steps.name: Thirty Tyrants
steps.what: Starving Athens surrenders, tears down the Long Walls and is put under a pro-Spartan oligarchy.
steps.why: The empire built on silver and ships was over.

stories.title: Alexander's march
stories.blurb: Where did Alexander go, and how did one army take the Persian Empire in about ten years?

steps.name: Accession of Alexander
steps.what: Philip II is murdered at Aegae and his 20-year-old son Alexander becomes king of Macedon.
steps.why: Alexander inherited his father's army and his planned war on Persia.

steps.name: Destruction of Thebes
steps.what: Alexander razes rebellious Thebes and enslaves its people.
steps.why: Terror secured Greece behind him before he crossed to Asia.

steps.name: Battle of the Granicus
steps.what: Alexander defeats the Persian satraps' army at a river crossing in northwest Anatolia.
steps.why: It opened Asia Minor and its Greek cities to him.

steps.name: Battle of Issus
steps.what: Alexander defeats Darius III, who flees, leaving his family in Macedonian hands.
steps.why: Darius lost the coast and the initiative.

steps.name: Siege of Tyre
steps.what: Alexander builds a causeway to island Tyre and takes it after about seven months.
steps.why: Taking the Phoenician ports neutralised the Persian fleet.

steps.name: Founding of Alexandria
steps.what: Alexander lays out a new Greek city on the coast of Egypt.
steps.why: Alexandria became the largest city of the Greek world and a centre of trade and learning.

steps.name: Visit to Siwa
steps.what: Alexander crosses the desert to the oracle of Ammon, which greets him as son of the god.
steps.why: It gave him a religious claim to rule Egypt and fed his image as more than a man.

steps.name: Battle of Gaugamela
steps.what: Alexander breaks Darius's much larger army on the plain east of the Tigris.
steps.why: The Persian Empire's central power was broken.
steps.date_note: date fixed by a lunar eclipse days before

steps.name: Burning of Persepolis
steps.what: Alexander loots the Persian treasuries and burns the palaces of Persepolis.
steps.why: Persian gold and silver, released as coin, changed the economy of the eastern Mediterranean.

steps.name: Death of Darius III
steps.what: Darius is killed by his own satrap Bessus while fleeing east, and Alexander claims his throne.
steps.why: Alexander now posed as the Persian king's heir.

steps.name: Alexandria Eschate
steps.what: Alexander founds 'Alexandria the Furthest' on the Syr Darya.
steps.why: Cities and garrisons were his way of holding Central Asia.

steps.name: Battle of the Hydaspes
steps.what: Alexander crosses the Jhelum and defeats King Porus and his war elephants.
steps.why: His last great battle carried the march into India.

steps.name: Mutiny at the Hyphasis
steps.what: Exhausted after eight years, his army refuses to go further east.
steps.why: The soldiers, not an enemy, set the limit of the empire.

steps.name: March through the Gedrosian desert
steps.what: Alexander leads part of the army back west through the Makran desert, losing many to heat and thirst.
steps.why: The return showed the cost of moving armies across empty land.

steps.name: Susa weddings
steps.what: Alexander and about 90 companions marry Persian noblewomen in a mass ceremony.
steps.why: He tried to fuse Macedonian and Persian elites into one ruling class.

steps.name: Death of Alexander
steps.what: Alexander dies in Babylon aged 32 after a short fever, with no adult heir.
steps.why: His generals carved the empire into Hellenistic kingdoms.

stories.title: From Warring States to Qin
stories.blurb: How did the state of Qin conquer its rivals and unify China, and why did its empire fall so fast?

steps.name: Battle of Jinyang
steps.what: The Zhao, Han and Wei families destroy the Zhi clan and divide the state of Jin among themselves.
steps.why: The Partition of Jin created the main rivals of the Warring States era.

steps.name: Reforms of Shang Yang
steps.what: Shang Yang reorganises Qin into households grouped for mutual responsibility, with ranks earned by military merit and land opened to farmers.
steps.why: Qin became a state built to grow grain and raise soldiers.

steps.name: Xianyang becomes capital
steps.what: Qin moves its capital to Xianyang on the Wei River and divides the state into counties run by appointed officials.
steps.why: Centralised counties replaced hereditary lords, a model later imposed on all China.

steps.name: Hu clothing and cavalry
steps.what: King Wuling of Zhao orders his soldiers to wear nomad-style trousers and fight as mounted archers.
steps.why: Warfare shifted toward mass armies and cavalry, raising the cost of survival for every state.

steps.name: Battle of Changping
steps.what: Qin's general Bai Qi surrounds the Zhao army; sources claim hundreds of thousands of prisoners were killed.
steps.why: Zhao, the last state able to match Qin in the field, was broken.

steps.name: Dujiangyan
steps.what: Qin's governor Li Bing builds a river works that splits the Min River to irrigate the Chengdu plain without a dam.
steps.why: Sichuan became a granary that fed Qin's armies; the system still works today.

steps.name: Zhengguo Canal
steps.what: A Han engineer builds a long irrigation canal across the Guanzhong plain.
steps.why: Han meant it to exhaust Qin; instead it made Qin's heartland richer.

steps.name: Qin unification
steps.what: Qi surrenders last, completing Qin's conquest of the six states; King Zheng takes the title First Emperor.
steps.why: For the first time all of the Chinese states were under one ruler.

steps.name: Standardisation under Qin
steps.what: Chancellor Li Si helps impose one script, one coinage, standard weights and measures and a fixed axle width.
steps.why: Common standards tied the conquered states into one economy and administration.

steps.name: Meng Tian's northern campaign
steps.what: General Meng Tian drives the Xiongnu from the Ordos and links older walls into a long northern frontier.
steps.why: The first Great Wall was built with conscripted labour at huge human cost.

steps.name: Lingqu Canal
steps.what: Qin builds a canal joining the Xiang and Li rivers to supply its armies in the far south.
steps.why: It linked the Yangtze and Pearl river systems for transport and conquest.

steps.name: Burning of books
steps.what: On Li Si's advice, private copies of histories and classics outside official use are ordered burned.
steps.why: Qin tried to control thought as tightly as land and labour.
steps.wikipedia: Burning of books and burying of scholars

steps.name: Death of Qin Shi Huang
steps.what: The First Emperor dies on a tour; Li Si and the eunuch Zhao Gao forge orders to put Huhai on the throne. He is buried at Mount Li with the terracotta army.
steps.why: The succession plot weakened the regime at its centre.

steps.name: Dazexiang uprising
steps.what: Conscripts delayed by rain, facing death for lateness under Qin law, rebel under Chen Sheng and Wu Guang.
steps.why: Harsh laws and labour demands turned subjects into rebels across the empire.
steps.wikipedia: Chen Sheng and Wu Guang uprising

steps.name: Battle of Julu
steps.what: Xiang Yu crushes the main Qin army in the north.
steps.why: Qin lost its last field army.

steps.name: Surrender of Ziying
steps.what: The last Qin ruler Ziying surrenders to Liu Bang; Xiang Yu later burns Xianyang.
steps.why: The dynasty that unified China lasted only 15 years, though its system outlived it in the Han.
